title: Power Distance and the Missing Voices in the Room
author: The Mindful Manager
summary: Opening with a small personal scene, watching his six-year-old go quiet and defer to an older Lego-club partner until a gentle 'what do you think?' gave him permission to speak, the author uses childhood status intimidation as an entry point into the workplace concept of power distance. He defines power distance precisely: when people perceive a gap in status, authority, or expertise, speaking up feels socially risky regardless of whether the senior person would actually welcome the challenge, meaning the effect operates on perception alone and can persist even when a leader genuinely wants dissent. He cites Wiley research finding only 53% of individual contributors feel safe taking risks at work, framing the resulting silence as a direct loss of challenge, creativity, and perspective for the organization. The piece then supplies three concrete tactics for leaders to actively reduce power distance: flattening hierarchy by shifting meeting framing from titles to roles, explicitly reinforcing a junior participant's specific credentials and reason for being in the room before a meeting, and inviting contribution through low-pressure, targeted questions followed by visible acknowledgment when someone does speak up. The closing reframe is the piece's sharpest point: most people don't lack a voice, they lack the conditions that make using their existing voice feel safe.
points: Defines power distance precisely as a perception-driven effect, not a reality-driven one: even a leader who genuinely welcomes challenge and debate will be met with silence if the people around them merely conclude that disagreement is risky.

Cites Wiley research finding only 53% of individual contributors feel safe taking risks at work, quantifying how much organizational challenge, creativity, and perspective is likely being lost to unaddressed status intimidation.

Prescribes 'flatten hierarchy' as a concrete first tactic: shifting meeting framing from job titles and org-chart position toward the specific role each person plays, which can reposition the most junior person in the room as the most relevant contributor.

Prescribes 'reinforce their credentials' as a second tactic: explicitly stating why a junior team member is in the room (closest to the client, deepest understanding of the challenge) before the meeting, rather than assuming their presence alone signals permission to speak.

Closes on a reframing insight distinguishing capability from confidence: 'people rarely need a voice, more often they need someone to create the conditions that make using it feel safe,' shifting responsibility for silence onto leaders rather than quiet participants.
quotes: What I needed were leaders who understood that when there's a perceived gap in status, authority or expertise, speaking up can feel risky. Not because people lack ideas, but because they're weighing up the social cost of sharing them.

What's interesting about power distance is that it doesn't need to be real to have an impact. It only needs to be perceived. A director may genuinely welcome challenge and debate, but if the people around them conclude that disagreement is risky, they'll stay quiet anyway.
Wiley's latest research found that only 53% of individual contributors feel safe taking risks at work. That means almost half are holding back in some way.
When you shift the focus from titles to roles, people become equals. In fact, the person at the bottom of that chart often moves right to the top.
Because people rarely need a voice. More often, they need someone to create the conditions that make using it feel safe.
